Money is defined as a medium of exchange. It is also, therefore, a useful measure of value. In a barter system, we trade like for non-like and make loose estimations of approximate value. 4 cows for a daughter (dowry, not slavery). A a few pounds of butter for an outfitting. Whatever it may be. But any of these things can become money, a medium of exchange, so long as they are sufficiently desired by a large enough number of people.

Essentially, whatever is universally valued, whatever is lightweight and easily transferrable, whatever retains its value over long periods of time, can become a medium of exchange; money.

So butter was once money. It doesn't rot as easily, it was universally valued, and it wasn't too difficult to bring to market and take back home. Feathers have been used as money, particularly amongst the native American Indians for the same reasons.

Gold follows this pattern: It is relatively light, compared to its sum total value. It is easily transferrable. It retains most of its value over time, despite chipping and abrasive wear. It is valued by many.

This is why cryptocurrencies are a valid alternative type of money. This is also why the U.S. Government has enforced the USD with oil contracts and military force. Paper has little value, but if they can enforce universal acceptance, then they are enforcing value upon it.

We can summarize a medium of exchange (money) as something durable with universally accepted value or worth.

Value. Value is a perception. Perceptions change. Pereceptions are dependent upon the perceiver. A perception is subject-object oriented. Now, let's reel it back in, a little.

How do people make money? That is, to say, how do people create value?

We own our thoughts and mind as property. We, therefore, own our bodies, which is the platform for containing our mind and thoughts. To continue, we need food and water and shelter (and love) to maintain the proper functioning and continued existence of our bodies. In fact, we need consistently applied food, water, and shelter (and love) to maintain the proper functioning and continued existence of our bodies.

According to John Locke, since we own our bodies, we can use that machinery to expand our influence of ownership. This is the Labor Theory of Property.

For example, if we (with our minds and bodies) choose to inhabit a structure (say, a cave) and we build and install a door, and we place some bedding, and we store our food, and we consistently maintain this, then we own it. It becomes our property by a principle of transference. We have "mixed our labor with the Earth" and become its steward. This initial investment grants us ownership status and the rights therein.

Likewise, if we discover an uninhabited plot of land and begin to till it. And we plant seeds and we water those seeds and nurture them for a season. Then we own the (literal and figurative) fruits of our labor. The produce belongs to us.

Since we own what we invest our time, effort, energy, and intellect into, we can decide what we do with the product of that investment. We can keep it, legally. We can defend it against intruders, thieves, and robbers. We can transfer it as a gift to our parents, lovers, children, friends. We can sell it; we can trade it for a goat or some butter or even gold. If someone wants it, they can have it, but only on our terms. The owner decides how a non-owner can acquire the good. It must be consensual; this is the nature of a contract with two (or more) signatures. Consent rules above all. Consent is the supreme law of the universe. If a non-owner acquires the good non-consensually, then they have committed a crime against person and property.

Back to the question: How do people make money?

In short, a person makes money when they, via their bodies and assets, create perceived value in others' eyes. In other words, I am rich when other people want what I have. More to the point: I am rich when others want what I have and I can give it to them in exchange for things that I want. Beauty, is truly, in the eye of the beholder.

Ok, two more things I want to touch up on:

What good is a barber who occasionally performs well and other times flubs it? What good is a farmer who makes tomatoes last year, grows nothing this year, and raises cows the next year? What good is a woman who is put-together today and disheveled tomorrow?

Well, they are a plenty good. Surely; for they produce what others value! But not as good as the barber who consistently performs well. Nor the farmer who consistently produces the same fruit. Nor the women who is onsistently kempt.

Even life, itself, requires consistently applied effort. In science, effort is measured in joules. And effort is called work. If I apply 1 pound's worth of joules in a downward direction upon a scale, then the scale will receive 1 pound's worth of joules in a downward direction, it will resist that effort and it will reflect the interaction as a 1 lb weight.

As a father, or a mother, what value are you to your children if you sometimes love them? What if some days they were not allowed into your house and became trespassers for entering and other days they were allowed in?

In love, what if your lover decided tomorrow that they no longer loved you? What if the next day, they loved you again?

When we show up to work daily, does our boss value us the same as if we showed up to work occasionally?

You see, even failure, is more highly valued when it can be relied upon.
